title: Atlas Ladder
basedOn: Ayn Rand’s philosophy, organized by topic. Short quotations are from her own works and are listed in SOURCES.md.

sections.title: Metaphysics
sections.summary: What exists, and what it is to exist. Volition is the top floor of this section, after the axioms, primacy, causality, and the metaphysically given.

units.title: Existence, Identity, Consciousness
units.summary: The three axioms and the formulas that state them.

lessons.title: Where philosophy starts
lessons.objective: Name Objectivism, the one-foot branches, and the three axiomatic concepts.

lessons.title: Existence exists
lessons.objective: Hold the first axiom: something is, and it does not depend on a wish.

lessons.title: A is A
lessons.objective: To exist is to be something. A contradiction is an error in thinking, not a feature of reality.

lessons.title: Consciousness
lessons.objective: Consciousness perceives what exists. Awareness with no object cancels itself.

lessons.title: One set of axioms
lessons.objective: Hold the three formulas together, and see why causality and primacy come next.

units.title: Primacy of Existence
units.summary: The universe exists independent of consciousness. Consciousness apprehends. It does not decree.

units.title: Causality as a Corollary of Identity
units.summary: The law of causality as the law of identity applied to action. A fuller floor than the preview you just climbed.

units.title: The Metaphysically Given
units.summary: Facts that are, as against facts that human choice brings into existence. What is given is not up for a vote.

units.title: Volition
units.summary: The primary choice to focus or not, and volition as axiomatic. This ladder places it after the metaphysically given.

sections.title: Epistemology
sections.summary: How you know. This section starts with the senses. Volition is on the metaphysics ladder.

units.title: The Validity of the Senses
units.summary: The senses as your only direct contact, percepts as the given, and the stolen-concept trap in attacking them.

lessons.title: The only direct contact
lessons.objective: The senses provide the material. Reason integrates it. Emotions do not replace either.

lessons.title: Percepts are the given
lessons.objective: You are aware of entities, not of free-floating sensations stored one by one.

lessons.title: The senses do not invent
lessons.objective: The organs have no volition to distort. The mind still has to identify what they give.

lessons.title: The stolen concept
lessons.objective: An attack on the senses that uses sensory evidence has stolen its own base.

lessons.title: From percept to reason
lessons.objective: Put the unit in one order: material, percept, identification, truth.

units.title: Concept-Formation and Measurement-Omission
units.summary: Differentiation, integration, and concepts as a mathematical process of measurement-omission.

units.title: Definitions and the Hierarchy
units.summary: Definition as the last step of concept-formation, and concepts as a hierarchy rather than a pile.

units.title: Objectivity
units.summary: Volitional adherence to reality by the method of logic. Knowledge as contextual and hierarchical.

units.title: Reason, Mysticism, and Skepticism
units.summary: Reason as the only means of knowledge, and mysticism and skepticism as denials of it.

units.title: Certainty and the Arbitrary
units.summary: The arbitrary as neither true nor false, and certainty as contextual.

sections.title: Human Nature
sections.summary: What kind of organism a human being is, once metaphysics and epistemology are in place.

units.title: Man as a Rational Animal
units.summary: Living organisms as goal-directed, and reason as the human means of survival.

units.title: Mind and Body
units.summary: No war between a ghostly mind and a mechanical body. Reason is an attribute of the individual.

units.title: Emotions as Products of Ideas
units.summary: Emotions as consequences of value-judgments, not as tools that discover facts.

units.title: Free Will and Character
units.summary: Character as the self you build by the choices you automate. A later floor, not a substitute for volition.

sections.title: Ethics
sections.summary: The code that guides choices, once you know what you are and how you know.

units.title: Why Man Needs Morality
units.summary: Why a code of values is a requirement of human life, not a decoration.

units.title: Life as the Standard
units.summary: Life as the root of value, and one’s own life as the standard of moral value.

units.title: The Three Cardinal Values
units.summary: Reason, purpose, and self-esteem.

units.title: The Seven Virtues
units.summary: Rationality, independence, integrity, honesty, justice, productiveness, and pride.

units.title: Happiness
units.summary: Happiness as the emotional state that follows from achieved values, not as a whim.

units.title: Egoism and Altruism
units.summary: The individual as the proper beneficiary of his own action, against the demand that he live for others.

sections.title: Politics
sections.summary: The social principles that follow when each person is an end in himself.

units.title: Individual Rights
units.summary: Rights as principles that sanction freedom of action in a social context.

units.title: The Initiation of Force
units.summary: Why starting the use of physical force is the basic political evil.

units.title: Government’s Proper Role
units.summary: Government as an agent that protects rights, limited to retaliatory force.

units.title: Capitalism and Its Moral Basis
units.summary: Laissez-faire capitalism as the system that follows from rights, not as a brute economic preference.

sections.title: Aesthetics
sections.summary: Art as a need of a conceptual consciousness, and the standards for judging it.

units.title: Art as Selective Re-creation
units.summary: Art as a selective re-creation of reality according to metaphysical value-judgments.

units.title: Sense of Life
units.summary: A sense of life as a pre-conceptual, emotional appraisal of man and of existence.

units.title: Romanticism
units.summary: Romanticism as the school committed to volition, and its place in Rand’s esthetics.

units.title: Esthetic Judgment
units.summary: How to judge a work by what it does as art, which is not the same as agreeing with its philosophy.

sections.title: Integration
sections.summary: The philosophy as one whole, and what it asks of a life.

units.title: The Philosophy as a Whole
units.summary: Why an idea pulled out of the middle cannot be validated or used.

units.title: Applying It
units.summary: Holding the principles in concrete choices, without turning the philosophy into a script.
